parsed.title: Autonomous Driving: End-to-End Learning, Imitation Learning, and Simulation
outline: Introduction to Deep Neural Networks in Autonomous Driving
End-to-End CNN vs Mid-Level RNN Approaches
Challenges and Limitations of Imitation Learning
Historical Data Collection and Model Foundations
parsed.markdown:
Autonomous driving research extensively employs deep neural networks for vehicle control, leveraging architectures such as convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and recurrent neural networks (RNNs) to process sensory inputs and generate driving commands [1, 2]. End-to-end CNN approaches, exemplified by DAVE-2, learn the entire processing pipeline from raw camera images to steering commands, benefiting from advances in neural architectures and training methods to effectively steer vehicles on public roads [1]. In contrast, methods like ChauffeurNet utilize RNNs with mid-level input and output representations, producing driving trajectories that are translated into control commands by a separate controller, facilitating training on both real and simulated data [2]. This fundamental methodological difference highlights a contradiction between direct control command generation and intermediate trajectory prediction in autonomous driving systems [1, 2].

Despite the promise of imitation learning, pure approaches face significant challenges such as error accumulation and distribution shift during closed-loop operation, which can lead to failures like getting stuck or collisions, even when trained on large datasets with mid-level representations [2]. These limitations underscore the necessity for complementary learning strategies or enhancements beyond pure imitation learning to achieve robust autonomous driving performance [2].

Simulation platforms like CARLA provide comprehensive support for autonomous driving research by offering open-source urban environments with flexible sensor configurations, diverse digital assets, and traffic rule compliance measurements [3]. CARLA enables controlled development, training, validation, and benchmarking of various autonomous driving approaches, including modular pipelines, end-to-end imitation learning, and reinforcement learning, allowing for closed-loop testing before real-world deployment [3]. This simulation environment addresses safety and reproducibility challenges inherent in real-world data collection and facilitates comparative evaluation of driving policies under standardized conditions [1, 2, 3].

The historical foundations of autonomous driving models trace back to projects such as DARPA's DAVE and the ALVINN system, with data collection efforts encompassing diverse roads, lighting, and weather conditions using camera-equipped vehicles driven by attentive human operators [1]. These early efforts laid the groundwork for modern end-to-end learning systems, which have progressively improved through increased data volume and computational power [1].

Current gaps in the field include the need for more reliable end-to-end neural network systems capable of replacing modular pipelines, particularly in challenging off-road scenarios, and effective solutions to mitigate error accumulation and distribution shift in closed-loop autonomous driving systems [1, 2]. Addressing these gaps is critical for advancing the robustness and practical deployment of autonomous vehicles.
